summary: Describes a distance-vector routing protocol for sending multicast datagrams through an internet. It is derived from RIP and implements the multicasting described in RFC 1054. It was experimental, and implementation was not recommended at that time.

plainLanguage.summary: DVMRP is an experimental routing protocol for sending IP multicast datagrams through an internetwork. It builds routes back toward sources and uses those routes to decide where to forward each datagram.

questions: how does dvmrp differ from rip
what is truncated reverse path broadcasting
subtitle: An experimental distance-vector method for routing multicast datagrams.

tldr.problem: The RFC notes that IP multicast had been described but lacked a routing protocol for use across networks.
tldr.mechanism: DVMRP adapts distance-vector routing to track paths back to multicast sources and uses Truncated Reverse Path Broadcasting to forward datagrams where group members may be reached.
tldr.outcome: The memo describes an experimental protocol and explicitly says implementation is not recommended at the time of publication.

today: RFC 1075 is an Experimental RFC published in November 1988. Its metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and its text says implementation is not recommended at the time of publication.

sections.title: DVMRP and Multicast Routing
sections.content:
The Distance Vector Multicast Routing Protocol (DVMRP) combines features of RIP with the Truncated Reverse Path Broadcasting algorithm. It is intended for use within an autonomous system, not between autonomous systems.

DVMRP tracks return paths to multicast sources. It is not designed to route ordinary unicast datagrams, so a router handling both kinds of traffic must use separate routing processes.
sections.plainLanguage: DVMRP helps routers deliver one datagram to members of a group. Its routes point toward the datagram's source, which helps routers decide whether an arriving packet followed the expected path.

sections.title: Messages and Route Updates
sections.content:
DVMRP uses IGMP to exchange routing datagrams. Each message has a fixed header and a stream of tagged commands, which carry route information or request routes. The tagged format allows commands to be added.

A DVMRP message is limited to 512 bytes, excluding the IP header. The memo defines commands for address families, subnet masks, metrics, flags, destinations, route requests, and experimental non-membership reports.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers exchange short messages that contain tagged instructions and route entries. A router can request route information or send neighbors updates about destinations.

sections.title: Tunnels Across Non-Multicast Networks
sections.content:
DVMRP describes tunnels between multicast routers separated by gateways that cannot route multicast. The tunnel carries a multicast datagram through a network that does not support multicast forwarding.

The RFC describes the tunnel as a transitional mechanism. The receiving router restores the original packet information after it arrives at the other end.
sections.plainLanguage: A tunnel carries a multicast packet between two multicast routers when the network between them cannot forward multicast. The router at the far end restores the packet for forwarding.

sections.title: Building Trees and Forwarding Datagrams
sections.content:
DVMRP uses distance-vector updates to learn paths toward source networks. Truncated Reverse Path Broadcasting builds a reverse-path tree and prunes branches that do not lead to group members.

For each multicast datagram, a router checks the source route and the incoming interface. It forwards copies along eligible interfaces, reducing the IP time-to-live for each copy and applying interface thresholds.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers build a tree of paths back toward each source. They forward a datagram only on branches that may lead to receivers, and discard packets that arrive from an unexpected direction.

sections.title: Timers and Operational Status
sections.content:
The protocol uses timers for route updates, group membership, and neighbor state. Configuration includes route metrics and interface thresholds; a threshold can limit whether a multicast packet leaves a network.

The document states that the protocol is experimental and that implementation is not recommended at the time it was written. It also notes that a link-state approach might provide a better basis for multicast routing.
sections.plainLanguage: Timers help routers decide when to refresh routes and when to stop treating a neighbor or group membership as active. The RFC presents DVMRP as an experiment, not as a recommended implementation.

references.text: Hedrick, C., "Routing Information Protocol", RFC 1058, June 1988.
